summary: A restatement of the Network Working Group's documentation conventions, updating RFC 3 on how notes in the series should be written and shared. It was itself replaced by RFC 16 and was updated by later notes in the same series (RFC 24, RFC 27 and RFC 30).

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 10 describes how the Network Working Group should write and share its notes. It encourages short, timely contributions, even when they are not polished or authoritative.

questions: what was the network working group
what were the early rfc documentation conventions
what could an nwg note contain
subtitle: Early rules for writing and distributing Network Working Group notes.

tldr.problem: The Network Working Group wanted to encourage timely discussion without treating every written note as authoritative.
tldr.mechanism: Anyone at any site could write a note related to network work; each note needed a number, author and affiliation, date, and title, then was distributed to a list of recipients.
tldr.outcome: RFC 10 revises RFC 3, was obsoleted by RFC 16, and was updated by RFCs 24, 27, and 30.

today: RFC 10 is obsoleted by RFC 16 and updates to it are recorded in RFC 24, RFC 27, and RFC 30. It also obsoletes RFC 3.

sections.title: The Network Working Group Notes
sections.content:
This note by S. Crocker, dated July 29, 1969, revises NWG/RFC 3. It describes the Network Working Group as concerned with HOST software, strategies for using the network, and early network experience.

Notes could be produced at any site by anyone and included in the series. Membership in the group was not closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The group used notes to share ideas about host software and the network. Anyone at any site could contribute a note.

sections.title: What a Note May Contain
sections.content:
A note may contain any thought or suggestion related to HOST software or another aspect of the network. The RFC encourages timeliness rather than polish, and says a note can be as short as one sentence.

It gives two reasons: written statements can be mistaken for authoritative positions, and people may hesitate to publish unpolished ideas. The conventions are intended to encourage discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: A note did not need to be complete or polished. The goal was to make it easier for people to share ideas for discussion.

sections.title: Information on Each Note
sections.content:
Each note should include the Network Working Group and Request for Comments labels with a serial number, the author's name and affiliation, a date, and a title. Titles do not need to be unique.

Steve Crocker at UCLA assigns the serial numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note needs a number, an author and affiliation, a date, and a title. The title can be reused.

sections.title: Distribution
sections.content:
The author sends one copy from their site to each person on the listed distribution list. The recipients include representatives at UCLA, UCSB, SRI, Utah, RAND, Lincoln Labs, BBN, ARPA, and SDC.

Recipients may reproduce the note locally if they want additional copies.
sections.plainLanguage: The author sends one copy to each listed recipient. Readers can make more copies locally.

references.text: NWG/RFC 3, the documentation conventions revised by this note.
